lead: This chapter introduces the two tools that keep values from changing — `const` and `constexpr` — and the two string types you will reach for in every subsequent chapter: `std::string` for text you own and modify, and `std::string_view` for text you only need to read. By the end you will be able to name every important constant in a program, understand the difference between values known at compile time and values fixed only at runtime, and choose correctly between `std::string` and `std::string_view` as function parameters and return types.

aids.title: const vs constexpr: the key difference
aids.md: Both `const` and `constexpr` prevent reassignment, but they answer different questions. `const` says "this value will not change after initialization" — the value may still come from a runtime call like `readAge()`. `constexpr` says "this value must be known at compile time" — the compiler will reject it if the initializer cannot be evaluated during compilation. When you need a named constant for things like array sizes or template arguments, reach for `constexpr`, not just `const`.

aids.title: Dangling views: the owner must outlive the viewer
aids.md: A `std::string_view` is just a pointer and a length pointing into memory owned by someone else. If that owner is destroyed — a local `std::string` goes out of scope, or a temporary created by `"text"s` is discarded — the view's pointer goes dangling and any use is undefined behavior. Safe views point at C-style string literals (which live for the whole program) or at a `std::string` that you can guarantee outlives the view.

aids.title: The leading-zero octal trap
aids.md: A leading `0` on an integer literal changes its base to octal: `012` is decimal 10, not 12. This is a silent, legal C++ pitfall — the compiler will not warn. In modern code, avoid leading zeros on integer literals unless you intend octal, and prefer the explicit `0b` prefix when you want binary.

aids.title: The leftover-newline problem with getline
aids.md: After `std::cin >> someInt`, a `'\n'` character remains in the input buffer. A subsequent `std::getline` call reads that leftover newline immediately and returns an empty string — a very common first-use bug. Fix it by writing `std::getline(std::cin >> std::ws, name)`: the `std::ws` manipulator discards leading whitespace (including that newline) before `getline` starts collecting text.

xrefs.md: Object-like macros (`#define MAX 30`) introduced in Chapter 2 are the older alternative to named constants; this lesson explains why `constexpr` variables are preferred over them.
